title: Goodnight Stories | The Singing Dough
subtitle: “Please don’t eat me. I’ll sing you beautiful songs.” — Hello, Li Yinhe
body:
## The Story Once upon a time there was an old woman who ran a breakfast stall. She sold neither fried dough sticks nor soy milk. Her little stall was filled with all kinds of pastries. Children loved the old woman’s pastry stall. The boys liked the little monster-shaped treats best, while the girls liked all the little animal-shaped ones.
One day, the old woman was almost out of dough. Only a little piece the size of a thumb remained. She was about to throw it away when she heard a bright, clear voice: “Please don’t eat me. I can sing you beautiful songs.” The old woman was startled. “Who’s speaking?” “It’s me.” The old woman rummaged in her pocket for a while, put on her reading glasses, and peered carefully at the stall. “Oh, it’s you, little dough.” “It’s me.”
The old woman remembered her good friend Jian from her youth. They had been so close then: going to school together, playing wildly together. If one fell ill, the other would not go to school either; she would pretend to be ill just to stay together. How had they drifted apart afterward? The old woman could not remember clearly. It seemed she had transferred schools, and being inseparable had turned into exchanging letters. Later still, she stopped receiving Jian’s letters. When she called to ask, it seemed Jian’s family had moved away too. “Then I’ll call you Little Jian.” “Yes, yes! Then let Little Jian sing you a song!” “Good child. What would you like to sing?” “Back then the sky was always so blue, and the days passed far too slowly. You always said graduation was a long way off; in the blink of an eye we went our separate ways…”[1] The little dough’s singing had the particular clarity of a child’s voice. The old woman began humming along.
Back then the sky was always so blue. Jian loved lying on the grass and looking at the sky. She herself was not so fond of looking at the sky, but reading beside Jian was a happy thing too. Sometimes she read her *The Little Prince*, and sometimes *The Red Lantern*. For a while, they both fell in love with Shakespeare and would laugh and talk their way through *Hamlet*, half reading, half acting. She loved watching Jian feign anguish while reciting the “to be or not to be” soliloquy, and loved competing to play the ghost for a while, to be the other’s father. More often, they did nothing at all, just lay on the grass. The sky was blue then, and the days really were slow. The little dough did not know the story of this song, but she had heard the old woman sing it many times, and sang it cheerfully. The old woman felt that being alone was indeed rather lonely. The next day, she shaped a swing for the little dough so that she could swing while singing. One person and one piece of dough kept running the little pastry stall. Their days were as plain as a glass of boiled water.
Until that day, when the little dough seemed to smell something sweet and sour in the air. That day, the old woman taught the little dough to sing: “We sit on the tall grain stacks, listening to Mother tell stories of the past.”[2] The little dough jumped off her swing. “Granny, I want to hear stories of the past too.” The old woman smiled. “Then what sort of stories would Little Jian like to hear?” “Little Jian would like to hear all your stories from all these years.” A cool, clear voice with a trace of tenderness sounded behind them. The little dough jumped. Who was that! How dare she impersonate her! “Y-you—how did you find this place?” “Oh, nothing much. I went to your old home, and everyone said you’d moved. Hardly any of the neighbors from back then could be found either. It was a little hard to find you, yes. But I thought, since I wanted to find you, even if I searched for ten years, for twenty years, I would surely find you.” The little dough smelled the sweetness of strawberries filling the air, perhaps with a little of the sweet tartness of oranges too. She was about to hop onto her swing for a better look when the old woman gently lifted her and put her into a little bed she had just shaped. “Grown-up matters are not for children to watch. Go to sleep.” The little dough felt terribly wronged. She had seen nothing at all.
She closed her eyes. In the darkness, she heard the sound of flowers opening.


## Afterword After reading *Hello, Li Yinhe*, I fell in love with Xiaobo’s ardent, moving expressions of love. So I borrowed and adapted his line, “Please don’t eat me. I’ll sing you beautiful songs,” to write this little story. I hope you who read it will like it. --- **Translator’s notes** [1] Lyrics quoted in the original from “My Deskmate” (同桌的你); translated here from the Chinese quotation. [2] Lyrics quoted in the original from “Listen to Mother Tell Stories of the Past” (听妈妈讲那过去的事情); translated here from the Chinese quotation.
